name: Cebu Taoist Temple
label: Taoist Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Canyon Road' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Canyon Road and Woolbright Drive (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1539233294: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cebu Taoist Temple' (175 m across).
notes: Colourful hillside temple in Beverly Hills with city views.

text.description: Cebu Taoist Temple is a bright red-and-gold temple on a hillside in the Beverly Hills subdivision. It was built in 1972 by Cebu's Chinese Filipino community and sits about 110 metres above sea level. It photographs well because the pagoda roofs, the long flight of steps and the wide view over the city all fit into one frame. The temple's stairs and pagoda rise above the road in the same view. This spot is said to be a quieter alternative to the crowded staircase, though the route comes from a 2011 report and may have changed since, so don't rely on it. The temple is open to worshippers and visitors alike, and devotees climb its 81 steps, one for each chapter of the Taoist scriptures. The entrance was built as a replica of the Great Wall of China. Once you are up at the temple, the dragon winding along the hillside and the tiered pagoda roofs make good foregrounds, with the coast and Mactan Island spread out below. Keep your phone outside the buildings: photography is not allowed inside the main hall and prayer halls, or of the saint statues. Visitors enter through a guardhouse where you need to show ID, so bring it with you. Opening hours vary, so check opening hours before you go.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in the Beverly Hills subdivision of Cebu City, on a hillside above the downtown area.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops nearby, so go by taxi or Grab from central Cebu City up into the Beverly Hills subdivision. Motorcycles can't enter, and you will need to show ID at the guardhouse. If you walk up from the guardhouse, Canyon Road is the sidewalk on the left at the turn into Woolbright Drive, though this route comes from a 2011 report and may have changed. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the stairs, the pagoda and the city view in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the temple. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Canyon Road and Woolbright Drive (sidewalk on the left at the turn into Woolbright Drive, on the approach to the temple). An open view across the sprawling city, Lapu-Lapu City and Mactan Island, with the temple's stairs and pagoda rising above the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pagoda on one of the upper lines, leaving the city and sea view in the lower part of the frame. Keep the road edge as a leading line. If you go up to the temple itself, a second shot is the green dragon in the foreground with the red-and-gold rooflines behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red and gold stay rich and the sky isn't washed out. Take a Live Photo if people are on the stairs, so you can choose the best frame afterwards. Remember that photography is not allowed inside the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the colourful roofs than midday does. Check the opening times first, as they differ between listings.

text.access_note: This is a working temple that welcomes visitors, reached through a guardhouse where you show ID, and photography is not allowed inside the main hall and prayer halls, so check opening hours before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Midday sun can be harsh on the bright red and gold surfaces.

name: Ayala Center Cebu
label: Ayala Center Cebu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Terraces, Ayala Center Cebu' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Yankee Candle At True Value Ayala Center Cebu' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4830868: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Mall and garden complex in the Business Park.

text.description: Ayala Center Cebu is the big shopping mall at the heart of the Cebu Business Park. For a phone photo, the best part is The Terraces, its open-air garden area, where a large tree and lots of greenery sit among modern buildings. It reads as a small green pocket in the city, and that contrast is what makes the picture. The upper balcony looks over the landscaped garden and the tree, and the view is wide and open, so it works at most times of day. The mall opened in November 1994 and was the first Ayala mall outside Metro Manila. The Terraces opened on 30 October 2008, on the site of the mall's old lagoon area, and now holds food and drink places. The mall is very busy, with more than 100,000 visitors on an average day and up to 160,000 at weekends. Expect people in your frame, and go early if you want it calmer. A major redevelopment of the mall, including its parks and gardens, was planned from 2024 to 2026, so the layout may differ from older photos. Stalls and events at The Terraces can block parts of the view, so look around for a clear angle before you shoot. If you want a second picture, the wide stairs and entrance, or the fountain against the greenery, make good alternatives.
text.geographic_location: Ayala Center Cebu is in the Cebu Business Park in Cebu City, and The Terraces is the open-air garden area within the mall. The subject is the mall itself.
text.directions_text: Head for the Cebu Business Park in Cebu City and look for Ayala Center Cebu. Once inside, follow the signs to The Terraces and go up to the upper balcony. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole garden, the tree and the buildings around it. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the tree canopy or people on the stairs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Terraces, Ayala Center Cebu (upper balcony overlooking the landscaped garden and the large tree). The mall's open-air garden with its large tree and greenery, framed by the surrounding modern architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the big tree on one of the third lines, with the buildings forming a frame around it. Keep the balcony rail low in the frame or out of it altogether. For a different shot, the wide stairs and entrance or the fountain against the greenery make good alternatives, and people add scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tree to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the greenery keeps its colour. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against the rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour (the hour after sunrise or before sunset) and after dark, when the decorative lights come on, are the best times. The wide, open view also works at other times of day.

text.access_note: The Terraces is part of a private shopping mall, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules on photography or professional shoots.

name: Magellan's Cross
label: Magellan's Cross
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Sugbo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Sugbo' (node/10250495182): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/94081127: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Magellan's Cross Pavilion' (19 m across).
notes: Christian cross planted in 1521, housed in a small pavilion with a painted ceiling.

text.description:
Magellan's Cross sits inside a small eight-sided kiosk of coral stone, built in 1834 under Spanish rule, on Plaza Sugbo beside the Basilica del Santo Niño. The pavilion houses the original wooden cross planted by Magellan's Spanish expedition when it reached Cebu on 21 April 1521, encased inside a tindalo-wood cross. The tindalo-wood case was placed around the original in 1835 to protect it from people chipping off pieces. Together with the basilica, the pavilion was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2021.

It photographs well because the arches work like picture frames. Stand just outside one and you get the cross in the middle, with the painted dome ceiling above it. The mural shows the baptism of Rajah Humabon and his household and the planting of the cross. The pavilion is small, so stepping back outside gives you a fuller picture than squeezing in. For a wider shot, move back across the plaza and include the whole pavilion with the basilica towers behind it. This puts the cross in its historic setting.

The pavilion has been closed to the general public since cracks appeared in the 2025 earthquake. People can still pray outside and see the cross through the entrances and windows. There may be scaffolding around the outside, so check the current situation before you go. Keep your phone steady, take a few frames, and be quiet and respectful around people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: Magellan's Cross is on Plaza Sugbo in Cebu City, right beside the Basilica del Santo Niño. Magallanes Street runs close by.
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or tram stop for this spot, so head for the Basilica del Santo Niño in Cebu City. The pavilion is on Plaza Sugbo, right next to the basilica. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from just outside an arch. It frames the cross and the ceiling together. If you want the whole pavilion with the basilica towers behind, step back across the plaza and switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). If railings, scaffolding or people are in the way, try 2x zoom to pick out the cross through the opening.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Sugbo (just outside one of the pavilion's arches, facing the cross). The wooden cross inside the octagonal coral-stone kiosk, framed by its arches with the painted dome ceiling visible above. Walk about a minute south-east to just outside one of the pavilion's arches and face the cross.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the cross inside the arch and let the stonework make a natural frame. Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the pavilion doesn't lean. For a different view, the wider shot from across Plaza Sugbo shows the whole facade with the basilica behind. Another option is Magallanes Street, which gives a street-level angle of the pavilion and the small chapel with the basilica close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cross to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky or plaza is washing out the stonework. Take a few frames in case people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The pavilion is a place of worship and a protected heritage site, and it is currently closed to the general public, so check the official site or the basilica before you go. Outside the pavilion, Plaza Sugbo is open and you can see the cross through the entrances and windows.

name: SM Seaside City
label: SM Seaside City
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sky Park' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sky Park' (way/610072128): middle (258 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/119432766: large area '' (1337 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large seafront mall with views of the bay and bridge.

text.description: SM Seaside City is a huge, circular shopping mall on Cebu's southern waterfront. It opened on 27 November 2015 and is the largest mall in Cebu, with a floor area of roughly 470,000 square metres. For a visitor with a phone, the best photo is not the building itself but the view from the top of it. Sky Park, the rooftop garden, gives a wide all-round scene. On one side the Cebu City skyline sits in front of the hills towards Busay. On the other side you look over the Mactan Channel to the CCLEX Bridge. The light is especially good in the late afternoon, before sunset, and the open sky gives you plenty of room to frame. Back at street level, the Cube is worth a quick picture. It is a 21 x 21 metre stainless steel sculpture in front of the mall, and the curve of the mall facade behind it fits into a wide-angle frame. For a calmer sea view, SRP Baywalk looks across the water to the bridge and is a pleasant place to watch the sky change colour. The tall tower at the centre of the mall is unoccupied and closed to visitors, so it cannot be used as a viewpoint. The view from Sky Park depends on the weather, so a clear afternoon is best.
text.geographic_location: SM Seaside City is in the South Road Properties area of Cebu City, on the Cebu South Coastal Road at the corner of F. Vestil Street. It faces the Mactan Channel.
text.directions_text: There is no Cebu rail or tram stop nearby, so head for the South Road Properties area of Cebu City and ask for SM Seaside City. Once inside the mall, follow the signs up to the rooftop garden, Sky Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyline and the bridge. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the rooftop garden, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the CCLEX Bridge or the hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (rooftop garden on top of the mall; the Cebu City skyline side faces Busay, the other side faces the Mactan Channel and CCLEX Bridge). A wide 360-degree rooftop scene with the city skyline and mountains on one side and the Mactan Channel with the CCLEX Bridge on the other. From there you get a wide all-round view. The centre of the mall lies a little to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, so the sky or the city fills most of the picture. Use the garden paths or planting in the foreground to add depth. For a different angle, try the Cube at street level in an ultra-wide shot with the curved mall facade behind it, or SRP Baywalk for an open view of the bridge across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Try panorama mode for the full sweep, moving the phone slowly and keeping it level. Tap the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich. Live Photos can catch a moving crowd or passing boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon leading up to sunset.

text.access_note: The mall is an open public space, but Sky Park access, mall hours and the paid Skywalk Adventure can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping gridlines on and the horizon on a grid line helps with straight, balanced framing.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep sky colours rich in late-afternoon light.

name: Basilica del Santo Niño
label: Santo Niño Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Magellan's Cross' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Magellan's Cross Pavilion' (way/94081127): middle (19 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/10757993558: the OpenStreetMap point 'Basilica Minore del Santo Niño de Cebu Pilgrim Center'.
notes: Oldest Roman Catholic church in the Philippines.

text.description:
The Basilica del Santo Niño is a Catholic minor basilica and the oldest church in the Philippines. It was founded in 1565 on the spot where the image of the Holy Child was rediscovered. The stone church you see today was completed in 1740. Its belfry and facade were badly damaged in the 2013 Bohol earthquake, and the bell tower was fully restored by October 2016.

The best-known photo here is not of the basilica alone. The companion shot is taken at Magellan's Cross, just outside the basilica, where you can photograph the cross in its wooden housing with the basilica's facade close behind. The cross and the church together tell the story of early Christian Cebu in one frame, and the two are only steps apart, so they fit into one short visit.

For the companion shot, keep the cross in the foreground and let the facade fill the background. If you have time, try a second angle. Plaza Hamabar gives a view of the bell tower and belfry, and the shaded Patio de San Juan suits facade details and portraits. The Pilgrim Center stands across from the basilica and is an open-air structure, so the compound can be busy when Masses are on. Go early on a weekday for softer light and fewer people.
text.geographic_location: In Cebu City, in the church compound where the Basilica del Santo Niño stands. Magellan's Cross is just outside the basilica, and the Pilgrim Center is opposite the basilica.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near this spot. The basilica is in Cebu City, so use the map to reach the church compound. Magellan's Cross is just outside the basilica, near the main entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cross with the facade behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole facade will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the belfry and facade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Magellan's Cross (just outside the basilica, a short walk from the main entrance). The enshrined cross in its wooden housing with the basilica's facade close behind, a classic historical backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and, for the companion shot, put the cross on one third of the frame, with the facade filling the rest. Hold the phone upright for height, or sideways if you want more of the plaza. For a different view, try Plaza Hamabar for the bell tower and belfry.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cross to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the facade. Wait a moment for people to move out of the shot. If you go inside, turn off flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early on a weekday for better light and smaller crowds. Avoid the Sinulog weekend unless you are attending.

text.access_note: The basilica is a working place of worship, and some parts of the complex, such as the museum and bell tower, may charge a small fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The basilica is in the historic centre of Cebu City.
Photography is generally allowed inside the basilica, but flash should be avoided and photos should not be taken during services.
Early weekday mornings usually have softer light and smaller crowds.
The Sinulog weekend is very crowded.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit a whole facade into the frame when standing close.
Modest dress is usually expected when entering a Catholic church.

name: Fort San Pedro
label: Fort San Pedro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort San Pedro' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/332819231: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort San Pedro' (169 m across).
notes: Spanish triangular bastion fort from 1738 by the waterfront.

text.description: Fort San Pedro is a small, solid stone fort on the Cebu waterfront, and it works well on a phone because its shapes are so clear. The walls are 6.1 metres high and 2.4 metres thick, and the fort is triangular, with two sides facing the sea and one facing the city. The stone is warm and pale, and it stands out against the grass and sky. Today's fort dates from 1738, and the date is carved on the gate alongside the coat of arms. It is described as the oldest triangular bastion fort in the country. It began as a wooden fort after Legazpi arrived in the 1560s, and it was later rebuilt in stone. In 2020 it was declared a National Cultural Treasure. Restoration used coral stone from the sea, which gives the walls their textured look. The best wide shot is from the grassy outer moat, looking towards the flagpole. The walls, flagpole and grass fall naturally into layers, so the frame feels balanced without much effort. For close-up details, such as the arched gate and its coat of arms, or the stonework, go in closer or use the telephoto lens. Once inside, the ramparts give a different view, looking out over the plaza and harbour. Some parts of the fort have been damaged by recent storms and earthquakes, so it is worth checking the official site before you visit.
text.geographic_location: Fort San Pedro is in the pier area of Cebu City, at Plaza Independencia, close to the harbour. A large statue of Legazpi and Pigafetta stands outside the fort walls.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed near the fort. The fort is in the Plaza Independencia area, in the pier area of the city, with two of its sides facing the sea. Head for Plaza Independencia, and once you are at the fort, walk round to the outer grassy moat on the outside of the walls. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view of the walls, flagpole and moat. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the fort's edges away from the corners of the frame so the walls don't lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the arched gate, the coat of arms and the stone texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, walk round to the outer grassy moat, which is the best place for the main shot, and face the flagpole. From here you get a wide view of the fort's walls and flagpole, with the grass of the moat in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the base of the walls along the lower third, with the grass filling the bottom of the picture and the flagpole standing clear against the sky. For a different shot, photograph the main entrance gate from the approach, framing the stone facade and the arch with its coat of arms. Once you're up on the ramparts, you can also look out across the plaza and harbour with the coral-stone walls in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't wash out. Take a few shots at different distances from the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone than midday sun. Check the fort's opening hours before you plan a visit.

text.access_note: The moat and plaza are outside the walls, but the ramparts and interior need an admission ticket and may have set opening hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone than midday sun.
The grassy moat can be photographed from outside the walls without paying admission.

name: Colon Street
label: Colon Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Colon Street corner with Mabini Street' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Colon Street and Mabini Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description: Colon Street is a historic street in downtown Cebu City, named after Cristóbal Colón (Christopher Columbus). It was once the heart of the city's shopping, offices and cinemas. Today it is busy, crowded and a bit run-down, which is part of its appeal for photographs: signs, shopfronts, vendors and passers-by make a lively scene. It is often called the oldest street in the Philippines, but historians dispute this. The earliest map showing it dates from 1873, and the 'oldest street' label seems to have started on postcards sold from 1910, so it is safest not to repeat the claim as settled fact in a caption. The best-known shot is the old postcard view: the grey obelisk in the foreground, with the street stretching away behind it. You can take the same view today, which makes a fun then-and-now comparison if you have an old print or an archive photo to hand. Move in closer on the obelisk and its markers for a more detailed picture, or step back to the arch that marks the start of the street. Since 2007 a night market has run here several times a year, mostly from September to January, so the street can look very different after dark. Crowds are part of the scene, so take your time and keep your phone secure in your hand or a zipped pocket.
text.geographic_location: Colon Street is in the downtown area of Cebu City.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Cebu City and ask for Colon Street. Once you are on the street, the obelisk is easy to spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the postcard view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the arch or a crowded stretch of street. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the obelisk and its markers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Colon Street and Mabini Street (standing across from the obelisk, facing down Colon). The obelisk in the foreground with the street stretching away behind it, framed the way early postcard photographers framed the old street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the obelisk on one of the vertical lines, with the street running away behind it. Keep the phone level so the shopfronts do not lean. For a different view, the obelisk in close-up shows its markers with vendors behind it. The Colon Street arch frames the start of the street with its shops and foot traffic beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the obelisk to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving through the frame. In the evening, night mode helps if you hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter. In the evening during the night market season, the street is busier and lit up, which makes a very different picture.

text.access_note: Colon Street is an open public street. Night market dates vary through the year, so bear that in mind if you plan to visit in the evening.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the street.
Night mode works better if the phone is held steady against something solid.
The obelisk can be seen from the corner with Mabini Street, with the street running away behind it.
The marked centre of the street is roughly 7 minutes on foot from the stand-here point.

name: Heritage of Cebu Monument
label: Heritage of Cebu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'P. Burgos Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of P. Burgos Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4161650691: the OpenStreetMap point 'Heritage of Cebu Monument'.
notes: Large sculpture telling the history of Cebu.

text.description:
The Heritage of Cebu Monument is a large sculpture tableau in the Parian district of downtown Cebu City. It tells the story of Cebu in bronze, brass, steel and concrete, from the Battle of Mactan in 1521 to the beatification of Pedro Calungsod in 2000. Scenes include the baptism of Rajah Humabon, a Spanish galleon, Magellan's Cross and models of well-known churches. The sculptor Eduardo Castrillo designed it, and it was inaugurated on 8 December 2000. It stands on the former Plaza Parian, where the old San Juan Bautista Church once was, and is the centrepiece of Parian Park.

It photographs well because it is packed with figures and detail, so even a simple wide shot looks busy and full of life. It is built to be walked around rather than seen from one spot, so plan on a few different pictures. Burgos Street. Then walk closer for details of individual scenes. If you have time, Parian Park gives a ground-level view of the church facade and the sculpted scenes. Go in daylight if you can, and keep an eye on your phone and bag as you would in any busy city area.
text.geographic_location: In the Parian district of downtown Cebu City, on the old Plaza Parian a short distance from the northern end of Colon Street, near Zulueta Street. It sits in a small triangular plot in Parian Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so get to the Parian area by road, near the northern end of Colon Street. Walk to P. From there the monument is about 220 m to the north, a short walk of roughly 3 minutes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view from the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want the whole tableau in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces, figures and the galleon without walking into other people's shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on P. Burgos Street (the view from the street toward the monument). The full monument as a wide view from the street, which is the classic framing shown on Wikipedia. Hold your phone level and keep the whole structure in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the verticals straight. Take one wide shot of the whole monument, then walk around it for close-ups of single scenes. For a different angle, Parian Park shows the church facade and sculpted scenes from the ground, framed by the park. Keep a little sky or street in the frame so the monument has some space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sculpture to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bright sky does not turn the bronze into a dark silhouette. If the lights are on in the evening, try night mode and hold the phone still against a wall or railing for a sharper shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening, when the light is softer and the monument may be lit up. Visit in daylight or with care after dark.

text.access_note: The monument stands in Parian Park, a public heritage setting with a fence around the monument; check the official site before you go for any access changes.

name: Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral
label: Cebu Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2692999: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main cathedral of the archdiocese with a tall bell tower.

text.description:
Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral is the seat of the Archdiocese of Cebu and is dedicated to Saint Vitalis of Milan. A church for this saint was first founded here in 1565, close to the Spanish fort, which makes this one of the oldest church sites in the Philippines. The building you see today is mostly a rebuild. Wartime bombing left only the bell tower (dated 1835), the façade and the walls standing, and the rest went up again in the 1950s. It looks squat and solid, with thick walls of the kind built to ride out typhoons. Look at the façade for the trefoil-shaped pediment, with its carved flowers, the IHS lettering and a pair of griffins, and for the Spanish royal coat of arms above the main door.

The obvious shot is the whole front from the open square. The quieter option, and the one this map's stand-here point favours, is the side garden beside the church. Green planting fills the foreground and the cathedral's stonework rises behind it, giving a softer, calmer picture with fewer people in it. Use the default lens (1x) for the garden and the wall together, and step closer to the plants to give the picture some depth. Keep your phone level with the gridlines switched on, so the walls do not lean. If you want the full front, the square is the alternative. Services may be under way inside, so be quiet and considerate with your phone.
text.geographic_location: In the downtown, south-eastern part of Cebu City, in the parish area that takes in Santo Niño, Parian and Tinago.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed near the cathedral, so head for downtown Cebu City and navigate to Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral on your map app. Once there, walk to the side of the church, where the garden is, and stand at the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the garden and the cathedral wall together. Switch to 2x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pick out the stonework without walking into the planting. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the front square, where it fits in the whole façade and bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see green garden planting in the foreground with the side of the cathedral's stonework behind it, a softer alternative to the front view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the plants low in the frame and let the cathedral wall fill the upper part. Turn on the gridlines and line the wall up with a vertical line so it stays straight. For the classic view instead, use the open front square, where the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens takes in the whole whitewashed façade with its pediment, cross and bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white walls keep their detail and don't wash out. Do not use flash, particularly if Mass is on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the sunlight is soft and warm, suits the garden and the stonework.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, and access may change because of restoration work, so check opening times before you go; photography is generally fine but avoid flash during Mass and do not fly a drone.

name: Casa Gorordo Museum
label: Casa Gorordo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Casa Gorordo Museum' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/721502852: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa Gorordo Museum' (47 m across).

text.description:
Casa Gorordo is a restored 19th-century house in the old Parian district of Cebu City. It was built in the 1850s by Alejandro Reynes y Rosales and later lived in by four generations of the Gorordo family, including Juan Gorordo, the first native Filipino bishop of Cebu. It is a classic balay nga tisa, a 'house with a tiled roof', and its look blends native Filipino, Spanish colonial and Chinese influences. The house came through World War II without structural damage, and the Ramon Aboitiz Foundation bought it in 1979. It opened in December 1983 as Cebu's first public museum.

It photographs well because of the textures: dark wood, stone, shell windows and warm period furniture. The best frame is from the second-floor balcony (veranda), where you can show the wooden upper floor and the house's details. If you have time, the shaded courtyard garden gives a softer, more open backdrop for the wood-and-stone architecture. Indoors, light through the translucent capiz shell windows falls on the old furniture and makes a moodier picture.

The photo spots are inside the museum, so expect to buy a ticket. Flash is discouraged or not allowed, some rooms do not permit photography, and commercial shoots need advance permission. Read the signs in each room and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Casa Gorordo Museum is in the Parian district, the old part of Cebu City. It sits in a museum compound that also holds the Kabilin Center, a gift shop and a courtyard cafe.
text.directions_text: No Cebu City rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Parian district in the old part of the city and ask for Casa Gorordo Museum by name. Once you arrive, the museum compound is the main thing to look for; go in through the entrance and head upstairs to the second-floor balcony. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the balcony and the house details. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in narrow rooms or to fit the whole veranda in. Use 2x telephoto if your phone has it, for carved wood and small details without leaning in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can photograph the wooden upper-floor balcony with the house's facade and details, looking out or along the veranda from inside the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the balcony rail or beams up with them so the wood looks straight. Include some of the veranda floor in the foreground to give a sense of depth. For a different picture, try the shaded courtyard garden with the house behind it, or hold the phone close to a capiz shell window to catch the glow on the furniture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Keep the flash off. Tap the brightest part of a window to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the shell windows keep their detail and the rooms stay warm. Hold the phone steady against a wall or rail instead of using night mode in dim rooms.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day, when natural light on the wooden balcony is softer and tour groups are usually smaller. Check the museum's opening hours before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum and the photo spots are inside, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules.

name: Carbon Market
label: Carbon Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Freedom Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Freedom Park' (way/1500196186): middle (123 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5037917: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Busy traditional market of fruit, fish and goods.

text.description:
Carbon Market is the largest market in Cebu City and the oldest in the Central Visayas region. It is a working market, so the pictures here are about everyday trade rather than neat scenery. Thousands of vendors sell fruit, vegetables, meat, clothing, kitchenware and handicrafts, and roving sellers work the nearby streets. The name comes from the Spanish word for coal, because the area once sat close to a coal depot for steamships and the old Cebu Railway.

The market is being rebuilt in phases. Freedom Park, the star-shaped plaza beside it, was restored in October 2022, and new market buildings are still under construction. That makes the park the easiest place for a wide shot. From the obelisk at the centre of the plaza you can put the monument in the foreground and let the market streets fill the background. It is open air, and you are not standing in the busy aisles.

For colour, walk over to the Carbon Interim Market, where the flower stalls and covered lanes suit close shots. F. Calderon Street gives street-level scenes of vendors and passing jeepneys. Ask vendors before you photograph them up close, and expect construction barriers to block some paths.
text.geographic_location: Carbon Market is in downtown Cebu City, in the Ermita area near the waterfront and the port. Freedom Park is the plaza right beside it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for downtown Cebu City near the port and Ermita, then walk to Freedom Park on the Magallanes Street side. Construction barriers may change the walking route, so follow the open paths. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the plaza, the obelisk and the market streets together. Use the default lens (1x) for street scenes and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as stalls and produce from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Freedom Park (obelisk at the centre of the star-shaped plaza, approached from the Magallanes Street edge). A wide view across the restored plaza toward the market district, with the obelisk in the foreground and the surrounding market streets beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the obelisk low in the frame and let the market streets sit behind it. Switch on the gridlines and keep the horizon level. For a different picture, try the Carbon Interim Market for flower stalls and covered lanes, or F. Calderon Street for vendors and jeepneys.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. In crowded lanes, Live Photos or a short burst helps you catch people mid-movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, when the market is likely to be busiest and most colourful. Avoid the hottest part of the day if you are shooting in the open plaza.

text.access_note: Freedom Park is an open public space, but redevelopment is ongoing and barriers may close paths, so check the official site before you go.

name: Museo Sugbo
label: Museo Sugbo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'M. J. Cuenco Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Toyota Cebu City - M. J. Cuenco' (pois); moved 30 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Provincial museum in the former Cebu jail.

text.description: Museo Sugbo is Cebu's provincial heritage museum, set in the old Cárcel de Cebú, the provincial jail of Cebu for well over a century. It photographs well because the building still looks like what it was: a heavy coral-stone front wall with arched, barred windows, which shows its age at a glance. The jail was designed in 1869 by Domingo de Escondrillas, and building began around 1871. It is believed that many of its coral blocks came from the Parian church, which was demolished in 1878. The first galleries opened in 2008, after the prisoners were moved to a newer complex in 2004. For the classic photo, cross M. J. Cuenco Avenue to the far sidewalk and face the front. The wall and windows fill most of the frame, and the historical marker on the near sidewalk gives you something in the foreground. Go before mid-morning if you can, because the light is best then. Inside the gate, the courtyard walls make a strong textured backdrop for a portrait or a detail shot, and two old cannons are reported beside the entrance, though that may have changed. Take the street shot first, then decide whether to go in. Photography is generally fine outdoors, but galleries often do not allow it, so ask at the entrance.
text.geographic_location: Museo Sugbo is at 731 M. J. Cuenco Avenue in the Tejero area of Cebu City. It is about four blocks from Plaza Independencia.
text.directions_text: Start from Plaza Independencia, which is about four blocks from the museum. No transit information is available, so use a map app to navigate to 731 M. J. Cuenco Avenue. Walk to the museum itself, cross to the far sidewalk of M. J. Cuenco Avenue, and face the museum front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the far sidewalk. If the wall is cut off at the sides, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). For details such as the windows or the marker, use 2x or more if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on M. J. Cuenco Avenue (far (opposite) sidewalk, facing the museum facade). The museum's coral-stone front wall and arched barred windows fill most of the frame, with the historical marker on the near sidewalk as a foreground anchor. J. J. Find the museum first and then cross the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the wall level so the arches do not lean. Place the marker low in the frame as a foreground anchor and let the wall fill the rest. For an alternative, go inside to the courtyard and use the old walls as a backdrop for a portrait or detail. You can also shoot the two cannons by the entrance with the front doors behind them, if they are still there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its texture. In the courtyard, try portrait mode for people in front of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just before 10am, when the sun lights the front head-on from the east.

text.access_note: The street view is from a public sidewalk, but the museum itself is a restricted-access site with opening days of Tuesday to Saturday. Admission may differ from what you expect, so check on the day and check the official site, including its photo rules.

name: Cebu Provincial Capitol
label: Provincial Capitol
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Osmeña Boulevard' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Osmeña Boulevard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5055817: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neoclassical government building with a dome.

text.description: Cebu Provincial Capitol is the seat of the province's government. It is a white neoclassical building with a dome on an octagonal drum, and it photographs well from Osmeña Boulevard, which leads up to it. It was designed by the Filipino architect Juan M. Arellano and finished in 1938, and the date MCMXXXVII is carved into the curved centre of the facade. The city plan behind it, drawn up in 1912, set Osmeña Boulevard as a grand avenue leading straight to the building. That is why a photo from the boulevard works so well: the road acts as a frame and your eye is led to the Capitol. Reviewers say it looks more impressive from the avenue than up close. The curved central balcony, the dome on its eight-sided base and the statues along the roofline are the details to look for. The building was declared a National Historical Landmark in 2008. It is a working government building, so treat this as an exterior photo stop. For a closer, fuller view of the front, N. Escario Street is a good second spot, where you can frame the whole white facade and entrance from the street.
text.geographic_location: The Capitol stands at the north end of Osmeña Boulevard in Cebu City, just beyond the Fuente Osmeña circle. Its main balcony and facade face the boulevard. N. Escario Street, near the corner with Gov. M. Roa, is another place to view the facade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head first to the Fuente Osmeña circle in central Cebu City. For the second view, walk round to N. Escario Street at the front of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the Capitol and the road in front of it together. Try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the building closer and make the street look compressed. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only from N. Escario Street, where you may be too close to fit the full facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Osmeña Boulevard (south end, looking north up the avenue after the Fuente Osmeña circle). The Capitol at the far end of the long boulevard, seen head-on as the building rises above the avenue. Look north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the Capitol on the centre line, with the nearby stretch of road running up into the picture so it leads the eye to the dome. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. As an alternative, from N. Escario Street frame the full white facade and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little if the white walls look washed out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white facade, and quieter traffic makes it easier to keep the road clear.

text.access_note: The grounds and facade can be photographed from outside, but this is a working government building and the interior is not open to tourists, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Museum of the Philippines – Cebu
label: National Museum Cebu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'A. Pigafetta Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of A. Pigafetta Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3385100: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Museum in the old Spanish-era Aduana building.

text.description: The National Museum of the Philippines – Cebu is housed in the old Aduana, the Customs House at the Port of Cebu City. It is a cream-coloured, two-storey building with a central tower and flagpole, and it photographs well from A. Pigafetta Street, where the facade is the building's own exhibit. The building went up in 1910 to house the Bureau of Customs and was designed by William E. Parsons, the Philippine government's architect from 1905 to 1914. It served as the Customs office until 2004. In 2019 it was declared a National Cultural Treasure. It was then converted into a museum, which opened to the public on 1 August 2023. For a phone photo, the best view is from A. Pigafetta Street, on the stretch facing the front facade. From there the tower sits in the middle of the frame, with the street in front of it. Morning is the best time, when the light falls directly on the front. If you have time, Plaza Independencia is reported as a quieter approach, but check the view from the park on the day. The courtyard, with its well and the building's columns and high walls, is also worth a look. Inside, rules on photography can differ from gallery to gallery, so follow the signs. One guide mentions that flash and videography are not allowed.
text.geographic_location: In central Cebu City, in the port area, at the edge of Plaza Independencia. The museum is in the former Customs House (Aduana) building, and the best front view is from A. Pigafetta Street.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops at this spot, so use a map app to reach Plaza Independencia, the park at whose edge the museum sits. From the plaza, walk to A. Pigafetta Street and stand on the stretch facing the museum's front facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and the building will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the tower and flagpole.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on A. Pigafetta Street (stretch facing the museum's front facade). The museum's cream, two-story Aduana (old Customs House) facade with its central tower and flagpole, framed against the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the tower and keep your phone level, so the walls do not lean. Include a little of the street in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different view, try the courtyard with its well and columns. Plaza Independencia is reported as a quieter approach, but check the view from the park on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with the centre vertical line. Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the cream walls look washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light hits the facade directly.

text.access_note: The museum is a public building and may have opening times, entry rules and photography rules inside, so check the official site before you go.

name: Plaza Independencia
label: Plaza Independencia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Independencia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Independencia' (way/242564999): middle (402 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q56062211: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Plaza Independencia is a Spanish colonial era plaza in Cebu City, and today it works as an open green space of lawns, mature trees and monuments. Over the centuries it has had several names, including Plaza de Armas, Plaza Mayor, Plaza de María Cristina and Plaza Libertad. The current name was adopted before the Second World War. The grounds include the triangular Fort San Pedro, a monument to the navigator Miguel López de Legazpi, a fountain, and memorials to Antonio Pigafetta, President Ramon Magsaysay and war veterans. The Pigafetta monument was restored in 2021. The plaza is a recognised heritage site.

It photographs well because it gives you simple layers: grass and trees in the middle, a fountain close to you, and stonework or monuments behind. Standing in the middle by the central fountain, you can frame the open lawns and trees with the fountain as a strong foreground shape. For a different view, the benches on the Fort San Pedro side look across the lawns toward the fort, with people sitting in the foreground. From M.J. Cuenco Avenue you can take a context shot of the plaza's frontage, with Fort San Pedro and the Malacañang sa Sugbo building beyond. Early morning and late afternoon give the softest light. Walk a slow circuit rather than shooting from one spot, because each monument is a separate small picture.
text.geographic_location: Plaza Independencia is in Cebu City, on the M.J. Cuenco Avenue frontage, with Fort San Pedro inside its grounds. The Malacañang sa Sugbo building can be seen beyond it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for Fort San Pedro and the M.J. Cuenco Avenue frontage in Cebu City. The plaza itself is about 1 minute on foot from there, to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the fountain, lawns and trees together. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view across the grass. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a monument or Fort San Pedro without walking up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Independencia (centre of the plaza, near the central fountain). The open lawns, mature trees and monuments of the plaza framed from its middle, with the fountain in the foreground. For a quieter alternative, sit on the Fort San Pedro side and shoot across the lawns toward the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on a lower third line, with trees and monuments filling the background. Keep the horizon level. For a context shot, step out to M.J. Cuenco Avenue and include the plaza frontage with Fort San Pedro and the Malacañang sa Sugbo building beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fountain to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. If the fountain is running, a Live Photo can catch the moving water. Use panorama only if you can keep your hands steady and few people are walking through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon give softer light, and golden hour before sunset is especially pleasant. If an event is on, the fountain may be lit, which can make a good evening shot.

text.access_note: The plaza appears to be an open public park, but check the official site before you go for any closures or photography restrictions, and for Fort San Pedro entry.

name: Yap–San Diego House
label: Yap-San Diego House
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q137776754: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: One of the oldest Chinese-Filipino residences, from the late 1600s.

text.description:
The Yap–San Diego House is a heritage house in the old Parián district of Cebu City. It is thought to be among the oldest surviving Chinese houses outside China, and one of the oldest homes in the Philippines. It was probably built between 1675 and 1700 by Don Juan Yap, a merchant from Fujian, and his wife Doña Maria Florido. Parián was the quarter where Chinese residents were required to live in Spanish colonial times.

It photographs well because it is a rare surviving piece of history with plenty of texture. The house has two storeys built of coral stone and wood, in the Bahay na bato style. It has windows on the upper level and a downward-sloping roof. The ground floor has an open-air garden. Together these give a phone camera plenty of texture to pick up.

The house is protected by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines and has been open to visitors since 2008. A descendant of the original family still looks after it, and a variety of historical artefacts are displayed inside.

For photos, start outside and take in the whole front, then move closer for the stone, the window frames and the roof edge. Inside, look for the garden and the displayed objects, and ask before taking photos indoors.
text.geographic_location: The house is in the historical Parián area of Cebu City, where Chinese residents were required to live in Spanish colonial times.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Parián area of Cebu City by taxi or hired scooter. Walk north from it to reach the front of the house. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the house. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too narrow to fit it in, and keep the house centred to limit stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the windows, the roof edge and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Mabini Street and Lopez Jaena Street (front facade at the corner, where the house's stone walls and the entrance meet the street). The two-storey coral-stone and wood house with its red Chinese lanterns and the large Santo Niño statue near the entrance, framed by the narrow Parian streets. Then walk up the street towards the house for closer shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the walls straight. Put the ground floor in the lower third and the windows and sloping roof above. Take one wide shot of the whole house, then close-ups of the texture. If the garden is open, frame it through the doorway to show the depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the stone and wood keep their colour. Indoors, use night mode if the rooms are dim, and hold the phone steady against a wall or doorframe.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front. Check locally for opening details and photography rules before you go.

text.access_note: The house has been open to the public since 2008, but check locally for opening arrangements, any entry rules and whether photography is allowed inside.
